speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right. Hon. Sir GEORGE PERLEY (Acting Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my sad duty to inform this house that another of our members has passed away, the hon. member for the constituency of Montmagny, who has been the Deputy Speaker of our house. Mr. LaVergne had a varied and colourful career. He was born at Arthabaska; he went to school there and in Montreal and, I think, in Ottawa also. He was very successful at school and at the university, where he studied law and graduated with honours. He was first elected to this House of Commons in

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
again on behalf of the official opposition I have to express to members of the government and hon. gentlemen opposite our sympathy in the loss of one of the members of their party. Again at this session we share their deep regret at the passing of one more of our number, particularly one who held the prominent position of Deputy Speaker in this chamber.
I believe it had long been apparent to all of us that Mr. Armand LaVergne, the late hon. member for Montmagny, was bearing with great fortitude very severe impairment to his health. It would be unfair and indeed impossible,, therefore, to attempt any estimate of his services to the public life of Canada by referring to the part with which we are most familiar and what we have known of him in this parliament. Personally, I like to go back in my remembrance of him to the days, to which reference has been made by my right hon. friend opposite, when as a

young man, almost, I should say, the youngest member, he entered parliament in the year 1904, and sat as a Liberal member of the Commons for the four following years. As the right hon. gentleman has truly said, the late hon. member was believed by all at that time to have before him a very promising career. He was an able debater and brilliant speaker. Even at that time he was an ardent advocate of more or less independent views. In 1908, as my right hon. friend has said, he resigned his seat in this house in order to enter the Quebec legislature, in which legislative body he served also for a period of four years.
In 1911 he was one of the organizers of the Nationalist party in the province of Quebec and, thereafter, a foremost member of that party; and in 1927 he was one of the Quebec organizers of the Conservative convention at Winnipeg. I believe the fact that in his day he was by turn a member of different political parties and, I fear, not very happy in his relations with any of them, accounts in part for the fact that although he was a candidate for parliament in all the political contests between 1911 and 1930, despite his attainments, it was not until 1930 that he was again returned as a member of this house.
It is very difficult to estimate the services to the public life of a country of those who too frequently alter their party allegiance, or of one who by his very nature is critical and independent in his views to the extent of finding it difficult to work with other men. I believe it is one of the laws of politics that we have all to learn to seek to accommodate our views to the views of those who belong to groups entertaining ideas similar to our own, if anything effective is to be accomplished. While undoubtedly it may be a mark of strength for one at all times to be wholly independent and outspoken in the expression of one's views, it is also at times an evidence of equal strength for one to be able, while holding and cherishing independent opinions, to cooperate with others differing somewhat in opinion but who are seeking to serve like national ends.
The late member for Montmagny achieved an enviable position in his profession of law, and also an important place in journalism. As a journalist, he was much given to expressing independent and, at times, extreme views. It is my opinion that the country will remember him for the zealous manner in which he upheld minority rights, particularly as they had to do with matters with w'hich he was deeply concerned. At all

Death of Armand LaVergne
times Mr. LaVergne was courageous and fearless, even to the extent of welcoming opposition and, upon occasions, of courting unpopularity. He will also be remembered for this, and, to those who knew him best, for qualities of heart and mind and for talents which, had he been less critical and more constructive and in some matters less eager perhaps to plough his solitary furrow, would have afforded him even wider spheres of public usefulness and national service.
1 join with the acting leader of the government on behalf of hon. members on this side, in the expression of sympathy which it is the desire of all should be conveyed by Your Honour to Madame LaVergne in her great bereavement.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is with deep regret the house has learned of the death of our former colleague from Montmagny. All hon. members will realize that as we have not had the pleasure of his company during the present session he must have been seriously ill. May I be permitted to join with the acting leader of the government (Sir George Perley) and the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in expressing from this corner of the chamber our deep regret of his passing, and our desire to convey through you, Mr. Speaker, to his widow and relatives our sincere respects.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I
add my personal tribute to the homage paid by the parliamentary leaders to the memory of our departed colleague. Armand LaVergne and I commenced our parliamentary career on the same day, in February, 1904. We have battled ever since, sometimes side by side, sometimes under different banners, and I cannot help feeling painfully shocked at the thought that Armand LaVergne is dead.
A true son of Quebec, he reflected throughout his entire life love of country, fidelity to traditions, the nobleness of our history and the joy of fighting in defence of what he loved. He always manifested an active devotion towards our land and towards our race, which he ever sought to keep conscious of its originality. Possessor of a caustic, original and supple mind, he never sought to conceal his thoughts. Quite properly was he known in days gone by as "l'enfant terrible" of Canadian politics.
Mr. Speaker, Armand LaVergne had reached the stage when one's thoughts turn no longer to the past, but to the future. His straightforward and lucid mind was too fond of clarity in matters pertaining to this world
not to seek the higher verities. He died as a true Christian, in the bosom of eternal truth. And our supreme farewell to him is the sad but confident one of those who believe, who hope and who love.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO THE MEMORY OF THE LATE DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I
add a word to what has just been said on the tomb of our departed friend. We were united, the member for Montmagny and I, by bonds of friendship dating from the time I left college, in 1908. Since then, we have followed sometimes the same path, sometimes different ones, but always have I held him, even when he was fighting us, in high respect and admiration. As a lawyer, Armand LaVergne was distinguished. In political life, he made a great name for himself. He was known in every province of the Dominion. An ardent patriot and a brave man, he was ever ready to defend the cause of minorities and to take up the cudgels for the oppressed. He conducted, for the rights of the French language, battles that will ever remain memorable. I think it can rightly be said that henceforth his name belongs to our history, to Canadian history and to the history of the French Canadian race. Likewise can we say of him what has been said of a man he greatly admired and of whom he frequently spoke: He was a knight without fear and without reproach.
To Mrs. LaVergne and to all his relatives and friends we extend our deep and sincere sympathy.

subtopic: BILL TO PROVIDE FOR THE APPOINTMENT OF AUDITORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked for information from the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) about Mr. Laforoe, one of the employees of the Canadian National Railways. In what I have to say I will be brief.
My intention is that not only the members of the railway and shipping committee are entitled to receive information from the Canadian National Railways, but also every member of this house who is called upon to vote moneys for the Canadian National Railways. I understand, of course, that some information may be confidential, but when I ask a question about the salary of a man and the kind of work he is doing for the railways, I am perfectly justified in doing so, and such a question calls for a reply, and a straight reply. We are ready to vote money for the Canadian National Railways when it is required, and we are entitled to receive all the information which is available. I have been most reasonable in asking for information in regard to the railways. In fact, this is the first question I have put this year with regard to them.
There is something I wish to tell the house about Mr. Laforoe. Here is a man employed by the railways for colonization purposes, and he is writing articles which are just like the exercises of a school boy, expatiating on the beauty of the country and all that. Furthermore, I am told that the publication of his articles in the press is paid for by other governments. Here is a man who is supposedly working for colonization. His salary is paid by the Canadian National Railways,

and his articles are paid for by the provincial governments. If the minister wants to practise economy in the Canadian National Railways the first thing he should do is discharge that man. Whenever I spoke in this house about distress in the different centres in the north the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) would come along with a telegram from that man saying that all was well, and the telegram was signed J. E. Laforce. I have mentioned that not only in this house, but I said the same thing in the parliament buildings of Quebec when the last congress on colonization was held there last fall.
I have received no answer to my question
about this man. Here is an opportunity for tlie minister to practise real economy. Let him see to it that the men who have been discharged from the railways, men who were doing good and useful work, are restored to their positions, and let him also see to it that all those who are doing nothing for the railways, and whose salaries are paid by the railway for doing nothing, are discharged at once.
I remember two years ago when I first brought up this matter it was at a morning sitting and the minister was right where he is sitting now. I advocated the same thing then, and the minister seemed to sympathize very much with my attitude.
With regard to the employees of the railway, Mr. Speaker, all the men who are doing useful work should be kept in their positions, but if you can dispense with a man who draws a big salary without doing useful work, and who draws that salary at the expense of three men who have the responsibilities of a family, that man should be laid off and the three men who could do useful work should be restored to their former positions. That is my humble view, and I submit it to the minister. I hope he will realize the stupidity of keeping on Mr. Laforce on the Canadian National Railways when no member of the house can get any information about his doings. I say that it is most unfair. The minister is fair enough to appreciate that. He probably will not admit it at once, but when he goes back to his office and thinks over what has just been said he will probably admit that the member for Temiscouata is following the right course in asking the minister to see to it that the greatest possible number of men are employed by the Canadian National Railways, and that all those who are drawing salaries for doing nothing shall be dispensed with at once.
There is another thing. What is the use of keeping as assistant superintendent at

C. N. R.-Auditors
Campbellton a man who can neither read nor write properly? It is just a fat job. What is he doing? The only thing he does is to try to put the greatest possible number of men out of their positions in order to justify his own salary. Is that economy? It is fattening one at the expense of many, and I ask most emphatically that his head be cut off. I do not say physically, but the house understands what I mean. There are many things like that, the purchase of materials for the railways, jam, lumber, construction materials of various kinds.

I will conclude my remarks with one sentence. Touche & Company have been auditors for some time. They have had a great deal of experience and they have not been criticized by the government for their work, which seems to me to have been
well done. On this we are all in perfect accord. But, sir, with regard to auditing, and strictly auditing, without getting into any questions of management, would it not be fair to see to it that Touche & Company do not join the ranks of the unemployed, but that they be given the most important duty of auditing the accounts of the Canadian Pacific Railway so that we may know what has been done with the $60,000,000 which has been lent by this government by order in council? That is my humble suggestion. I suggest that the government avail themselves of the experience of this firm in having the finances of the Canadian Pacific Railway thoroughly audited by Touche & Company.

subtopic: BILL TO PROVIDE FOR THE APPOINTMENT OF AUDITORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since yon have allowed the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) to ramble out of order, may I be permitted for a minute or two to say a word in defence of Mr. Laforce. I have known Mr. Laforce for many years, have followed his work, and can say without hesitation that he is a competent official in his department. It seems to me that when we have competent officials we should retain them. But if the attitude advocated by my hon. friend from Temiscouata is to be adopted, and Mr. Laforce is to be dismissed, notwithstanding that everyone who has come in contact with him knows how well he is doing his work, it is simply following the method of the present government. The minister said the other day that the auditors of Touche & Company were very competent and that the work was well done, and yet we are dismissing them. I think it is a wrong attitude. If the officials of any railway company over which we have control are doing their work properly-and I know that Mr. Laforce has rendered valuable service from the colonization standpoint-then I think it ill becomes the government to dismiss any official, or any group of officials who have given such services as those rendered by Touche & Company as auditors for the Canadian National Railways.

speechtext:
AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT act, 1934
The house resumed from Monday, March 4, consideration in committee of Bill No. 10, to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934-Mr. Rhodes-Mr. Bury in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We finished the clauses of the bill when last in committee, but the hon. member for Macleod had submitted an amendment which had been ruled out of order, and then he proposed! submitting a portion of the original amendment as an amendment. I am prepared to speak on that if my hon. friend desires to proceed.

If I remember rightly, Hansard will show that I formally moved a second amendment last night, and I do not think it is necessary to say anything further in support of it. As I have said in this committee so many times, the present level of farm prices makes it impossible for farmers to pay a rate of interest higher than five per cent. Perhaps I am setting the rate very high when I place it at five per cent, but I might direct the attention of the committee to section 17 of the act of last year, which I think includes the principle covered in the amendment. Section 17 of the act as introduced by the Prime Minister last year reads:
(1) Notwithstanding the provisions of any other statute or law, whenever any rate of interest exceeding seven per centum is stipulated for in any mortgage of farm real estate, if any person liable to pay the mortgage tenders or pays to the person entitled to receive the money, the amount owing on such mortgage and interest to the time of payment, together with three months' further interest in lieu of notice, no interest shall after the expiry of three months' period aforesaid be chargeable, payable or recoverable in respect of the said mortgage at any rate in excess of five per centum per annum.
2. The provisions of this section shall apply in the case of any mortgage heretofore or hereafter made and whether or not the principal sum is due and owing at the time such tender or payment is made.
The principle of reducing the rate of interest on existing mortgages to five per cent is included in that section. It is true that this is applied only in the case of any mortgagor who is able to tender payment of the full principal sum as well as any interest which may be owing, but after all it seems to me that th^t does not alter the principle that the rate of interest on farm mortgages should not exceed five per cent per annum.

Might I point out to the committee that although this act did not come into force in any province until proclaimed by the governor in council to be in force in such province, section 17 which I have just quoted came into force when the act was assented to. That was the one section of the act which came into force immediately the act was given royal assent; all the other sections did not apply in any province until a proclamation to that effect was issued. I think that point should not be overlooked in considering the amendment which is now before the committee and which asks that:
No interest at a rate exceeding five per centum per annum shall be charged, payable or recoverable on any existing mortgage of farm real estate or agreement covering the sale of farm real estate.
I would not press this amendment again on the committee were it not for the fact that I realize how badly it is needed. I believe the government, the House of Commons and the committee would pass this amendment if they appreciated, as some of us do, the need for it and how agriculturists as a whole cannot stand the present rate of interest.
Why should this be confined to mortgages in connection with purchase of property? Why should it not apply to all farm mortgages?

It applies to all farm mortgages. It reads:
No interest at a rate exceeding five per centum per annum shall be charged, payable or recoverable on any existing mortgage of farm real estate or agreement covering the sale of farm real estate.
The amendment covers both.
I would also like to remind the committee that, as I said yesterday, almost every agricultural country I know of has passed legislation of this nature effecting a general reduction in the interest rate on farm mortgages. At the moment I do not know of any other country, although there may be such, where it is permissible to collect a rate of interest of more than five per cent on farm mortgages. I do not think we can afford any longer to delay taking action to reduce the interest rate on farm mortgages. As I said last night only a small percentage of the farmers will take advantage of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and as this act deals with the particular question of farm debts, it is very important and necessary and there is a responsibility on this committee to see that some provision of this nature is included in the act or that legislation is passed at some time during this session respecting reduction of

Farmers' Creditors Act
interest rates charged on farm mortgages generally. I hope the committee will accept the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will all concede at onice to the hon. member for Macleod that he is animated toy sincerity of purpose and that it is his desire to accomplish something by way of reduction of interest. It may rather surprise him to know I have a sympathetic feeling for the object he has in mind, but if I were discussing the merits I would say that we must 'be .practical about these matters. It would be very easy, if it were competent for the committee, under the amendment of my hon. friend to say that the interest shall be only so much. Last year I used the illustration and I might use it now, that it is an old maxim that you may lead a horse to water but you cannot make him drink. iH you get the rate of interest below the point where lenders are prepared to lend, then there will be no money available, and if a farmer is in dire need of money he will be the sufferer in the long run.
But I do not propose to enter into the merits of the discussion for reasons which I shall disclose in a moment, because there will be another opportunity during this session. My hon. friend's amendment reads:
No interest at a rate exceeding five per centum per annum shall be charged, payable or recoverable on any existing mortgage of farm real estate or agreement covering the sale of farm real estate.
May I point out at once that at this moment we are under the farm loan board loaning money at five and a half per cent. I have stated before and have no hesitation in stating again that I hope to see that rate reduced to five per cent and possibly lower. But the point is that not only are we at the moment making new loans at that rate, but we have many millions loaned under the old Farm Loan Act paying six and a half per cent, which under the legislation that is now before the committee we shall have an opportunity of reducing to a lower rate after the bill is passed. In the meantime however those mortgages are out at six and a half per cent. The effect of my hon. friend's amendment is to make a direct charge upon the public revenue, because the deficiency will have to be made up out of the exchequer, and I submit as a point of order that upon that ground it is not competent for my hon. friend to move this amendment.
II submit that the amendment is out of order for another reason. My hon. friend introduced into the house at this very session a bill which passed its second reading and
which is now before the banking and commerce committee. Paragraph 5a of clause 4 of that bill, to amend the interest rate, reads:
In no case shall interest exceeding the rate or percentage of four per centum per annum be stipulated for, charged, taken, payable or recoverable on the whole or any part of the principal money advanced on or secured by mortgage of real estate, or on moneys payable under agreements for sale of real estate.
That very subject is now before a committee of this house. May I further point out that the amendment which my hon. friend now moves is much less in scope than is the clause of the bill which I have just read, because the clause of the bill refers to all mortgages whereas the amendment which my hon. friend now moves refers only to farm mortgages. Inasmuch as the lesser is included in the whole, this very subject will be determined when the bill is dealt with by the banking and commerce committee and comes back to this house for final action. But 1 do not stress the point of order although 1 feel it my duty to raise it on that point as well. I submit this however as a practical proposal: Is it wise to attempt to deal with legislation piecemeal? Is it wise to attempt to deal with a limited scope of farm mortgages when at this very session we are dealing with a bill which has reference to the interest rate upon all mortgages? Under these circumstances, in view of the fact that this subject will be decided upon, I hope my hon. friend will not press his motion.
I must confess that I have a great deal of sympathy with the proposed amendment for more than one reason. Did I understand that my hon. friend is pressing his point of order?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I must, unless the amendment is withdrawn.

Then my remarks must be very brief; perhaps I shall be able to conclude them on another occasion. The whole purpose of this bill is to relieve a desperate situation; I think that is not putting it in too strong language. I cannot conceive that any arrangement will get a farmer-who after all has the choice between a compromise and becoming a bankrupt-out of his difficulty if he has to pay a rate higher than five per cent. I agree that our direction to the boards and to the registrar in dealing with the matter should be as wide as possible; for circumstances will vary. But at the same time if I were a member of a board and were adjudicating upon a claim in which the interest rate for a period of two or three years was
Farmers' Creditors Act

going to be more than five per cent, no matter how much the reduction in principal, it seems to me that there would be very little likelihood of the debtor being able to meet his obligation. That is my opinion. I appreciate that the matter should be left entirely to the discretion of the board, it must of necessity be so, but at the same time my hon. friend knows the conditions existing not only in western Canada but all over Canada to-day and that probably will exist for the next three or four years. The hope is that the adjustment granted will put the debtor in a position to meet his obligation, but it is my candid opinion that he cannot pay more than five per cent interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I say at once to my
hon. friend that I do not quarrel with the general tenor of his remarks, but I point out that if this bill were silent altogether upon the question of interest the effect would be precisely the same as if this clause or any other were placed in the bill; because in the first place it would not interfere with the debtor and creditor getting together and agreeing to a compromise, nor would it prevent the board of review from fixing a rate of interest. So that I feel that it is not incumbent upon us at the moment to deal with the question of interest at all. The whole spirit of this act, as my hon. friend properly points out, is that of conciliation and compromise. 'Let us preserve that spirit.
The hon. member for Macleod referred to section 17 of the present act. 'Last night I was at pains to read the remarks of the Prime Minister who piloted that act through the house, and I found that the object of section 17 was not interest, but to compel mortgagees who held mortgages carrying rates as high as eight and nine per cent and who ' refused to take payment of the mortgage in times when the farmers were prosperous and could have paid them, to accept repayment of the principal. That three months clause was placed there to compel the mortgagee to take his money if tendered. It was not so much the matter of interest that was in mind in inserting that clause.
Is the minister referring to an overdue payment of principal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I am referring to section 17 of the farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, which was placed in the act, I say, for the purpose of compelling mortgagees to accept payment of the principal of a mortgage carrying a high rate of interest. If

my hon. friend is interested I refer him to the remarks of the Prime Minister to be found at page 3640 of Hansard of last year, in which he outlined the reasons for putting that provision in the bill. As I said, there is no object in discussing the merits of the proposed amendment now, and this is not evasion on my part. Of course I want to see the procedure properly observed and our business conducted in an orderly fashion. But this whole question of interest is being dealt with by a bill which is now before the house, and if it passes it will have precisely the same effect as if we inserted a clause in the present bill dealing with the subject of interest, but will apply to the wider sphere of mortgages in general.

I do not
wish to delay the passing of the bill, but I do not view the matter in the same light as the minister. This is a special piece of legislation.	The bill introduced by the hon.
member for Macleod is general in its application. I think that is where he went astray yesterday in his proposed amendment. The bill we are going to consider deals with all mortgages; this is a special piece of legislation for a special purpose, hence my interest in seeing a reasonable rate of interest specified in it. I quite admit that much must be left to the discretion of the board, but I point out that this is special legislation and does not touch the general situation at all, while the other bill is very wide in its effect, for it relates to all mortgages.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Including this. My hon.
friend overlooks the fact that inasmuch as Bill No. 11 is wider in its application it includes what is dealt with in this bill. Surely we are not going to have two laws on the one subject.

Might it not happen that
the house would pass the present bill but reject the wider one? If we miss the chance of giving them half in the hope of giving them all and in the result give them nothing, it would not be wise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

If my hon. friend means
by giving the whole that there will be a decision with respect to Bill No. 11 and that it will come back before this house, I will say yes, we will get the whole. What my hon. friend is overlooking is that the question of interest has nothing to do with the settlement of debts provided for under this bill. I have seen settlements in which interest at as low as three per cent was agreed to between debtor and creditor, where the original obligation was for a rate as high as six per cent.

are the last great agricultural country in the world to deal with it, and it seems to me this is the time to deal with it, in connection with this act.
It may be that I am wrong in this. The minister may be perfectly sincere; let us grant that we are both sincere. I feel this is the proper place to deal with this matter, because this act deals with the specific question of farm debts. Again I urge the committee, and the minister, that we should be allowed to decide this question now, whether five per cent is a proper rate; I think this is a very good place to decide it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend in his sincerity of purpose and with all proper motives, which I accord to him-although I regret to say that he showed some hesitancy in conceding that I might be animated by equally worthy motives-will insist on discussing the merits of the question. I have stated before that I am not doing that now, inasmuch as we will do so before this parliament concludes. My hon. friend speaks for the farmer who is not going to come under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. That farmer will get such protection as this house may decide to accord him when it deals with Bill No. 11, which covers all mortgages.
Apart from the question of procedure, on which I am going to ask the chair to rule, I submit that at this moment my hon. friend is asking the committee to pass an amendment saying that the interest on farm mortgages should be limited to five per cent while at the same time he has a bill before the committee on banking and commerce, which has had second reading, which provides that all mortgages including farm mortgages shall bear a rate of interest not exceeding four per cent. Look at the logic of that position, and its consistency. My hon. friend is going to ask the farmers in one bill to pay one per cent more than they would pay under another bill. He is going to limit the rate on all mortgages to four per cent with the exception of farm mortgages which, under another bill, are to pay five per cent. Inasmuch as we are going to deal with this question in connection with Bill No. 11 which will cover all mortgages including those on farms, from a practical point of view I submit that we should confine our efforts in that direction to Bill No. 11.
Does the hon. member press for a ruling?
No, I do not press for a ruling. I do hope the committee will accept my amendment, though.

If the hon. member presses I must rule, and my ruling will be that the amendment is out of order for two reasons, first, that it involves the revenues of the crown and second that it is part of an amendment which itself, as a whole, was ruled out of order.

Mr. Chairman, before the -bill is reported I should like once more to bring to the attention of members of the committee and of the government the suggestion that there should be a definite date of conclusion for this legislation. Yesterday we learned that only a very small1 percentage of our farmers have as yet taken advantage of the opportunity afforded them undeT this legislation. For purposes of argument let us assume that ten times as m-anry farmers in Canada will take advantage of this measure. Surely it is not the intention that this legislation- should be continued indefinitely; surely the intention was that it should be for the protection of the farmers who at present are unable to discharge their obligations; surely it was not the intention that it should take care of farmers during the next three, four or five years. I submit to the members of the committee that to-day farmers throughout Canada are having difficulty in securing credit for the small amounts of money they require in order to conduct their business, by virtue of this legislation in conjunction with the moratoria existing in the various provinces of Canada.
I suggest to the minister again that he seriously consider at this time bringing in an amendment setting some definite limit. I think any farmer who is not in a position to discharge his obligations to-day, or six months or nine .months from now, should be able to take advantage of this legislation, but we will injure the standing of the farmer in the community and we will harm his credit unless something is done to terminate this legislation at the end of some definite period. I believe in the interests of the farmers themselves and in the interests of those we are trying to help by this legislation the minister, before this measure is given third reading, should bring in an amendment to terminate it at some definite date.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not know that my hon. friend had risen and wished to speak, but I should be quite content to allow him to do so. I was only going to reply to my hon. friend from Vancouver-Burrard, not because il have any keen and eager desire to be continuously upon my feet but because I wish to do each hon. member who makes a specific proposal the courtesy of giving him an answer. I was going to say that I would deprecate any suggestion that this should be regarded as continuing and all-time legislation. It is designed, admittedly, to meet a set of circumstances which we hope will never recur -certainly not within the lifetime of the youngest member of this house. But at the moment it would be a mistake to attempt to put on a time limit. If we were to put on a time limit which was too short we would be shutting out a number of worthy farmers who perhaps would not have the opportunity to have their cases considered. If we made it too long we would serve to aggravate the idea the hon. member has quite properly expressed, namely that it would serve to disturb conditions, and would result in affecting the credit of the farmer.
May I point out that in all probability the next session would give ample time to deal with this matter. But even assuming that the act has served its full purpose prior to the next session the remedy lies in the hands of the government, because all it has to do is to dismantle the machinery and the act cannot function. We know that unless there be official receivers, a registrar and a board of review it cannot function. For these reasons I respectfully submit the matter is one which ought to remain over at least until another session of parliament.

In response to the minister I should like to submit a suggestion that any farmers who are in a position where they may wish at this time or in the near future to take advantage of this legislation, could very well do so, and they will do so if there is a definite date for conclusion. But if the hope is held out to them that in a year, two years or two years and a half they may still come under this legislation they will not act at the present time. I think it would be advisable to learn now just where we stand. How many of our farmers require this relief? Instead of leaving the matter over till the next session of parliament, or leaving it with the government to take a responsibility which we feel they would never take, namely that of dismantling the machinery, I believe we might very well move an amendment to the bill so that one
year from now it may be terminated, and if at the end of that time we find it necessary to renew the legislation, then I think we might do so. I believe the method I have suggested would be better than the one suggested by the minister.
I would remind the committee that there is nothing before the chair.

I believe there is some misapprehension in the mind of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. A few days ago he referred to the legislation before us as class legislation. He will discover that it is equalizing legislation. The Bankruptcy Act applies to every person in Canada, with the exception of the farmer. In no province in the dominion may a farmer be put into bankruptcy. In the province of Quebec a f armer may not put himself into bankruptcy. This legislation merely places the farmer in the position occupied by the trader and the manufacturer. It gives the farmer the privilege of shedding his debts, if he cannot pay them, and places him on an equality or on an equal footing with other classes in the community. I submit- it does nothing more.

This discussion is entirely out of order; there is nothing before the chair. Hon. members may speak on third reading, and at that time make any further observations they may choose to make. But they are out of order now.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister a question.
Order.

My desire is to ask the minister one question before the bill leaves the committee. To what extent does the farmer debtor require to default in the payment of either principal or interest before he is eligible to appear before the various tribunals for redress? Must it be to the extent of defaulted interest, prinioipal, or both or either-or is there any extent?

Well, if a debtor is behind say one year's interest he is eligible to appear?

speechtext: Yes.

you report the bill. . . .

I do not think it is out of order.

Mr. Chairman, before you report this bill, I simply want to move an amendment, without adding any observations on the different sections that have been adopted. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) that the following clause be added to the bill:

I never heard of it
Neither did I.

Well then, what has the chairman been allowing us to discuss for the last hour?
The CHAIRMAN (Mr. Bury? It should not have been allowed.

If the chairman, has been

The chairman was magnanimous because the discussion began towards the close of the last sitting of the committee.

With all due respect to the chairman-and I should not like to be disrespectful-I submit that is hardly a justification for having allowed the discussion to carry on all afternoon. If the hon. member for Joliette wishes at this time to move an additional clause to the bill I can see no reason why he should be precluded fiom doing so.

Mr. Chairman, I understand that by unanimous consent the house is sitting in committee to consider part of Bill No. 10. So, if we are authorized by unanimous consent to consider the bill, I fail to see why I should not be permitted to move an amendment thereto.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have been relying upon
the ruling of the chair, because without consulting authorities I do not feel competent to express an opinion as to whether or not the ruling is correct. I have no doubt, however, that it must be because he has the authority before him. Whether or not a correct ruling has been made I submit to the hon. member moving the amendment that I ought at least to have had extended to me the courtesy of being supplied with a copy. I do not know what the amendment contains.

If it is
the will of the committee the amendment may be moved. Is it the will of the committee that the hon. member have leave to move the amendment?

In my
opinion, Mr. Chairman, he does not require the leave of the committee to introduce his amendment. That is an absurdity because at any stage of the proceedings on any bill any hon. member has the right to move any amendment to it. It is really reducing the

Farmers' Creditors Act
rules to utter ridiculousness if we are going to submit to this sort of ruling. It will simply mean that the amendment will be moved on the third reading. So neither the house nor the committee nor the chairman is going to get anywhere by making rulings of this sort.
Apparently it is the will of the committee that the hon. gentleman should proceed.

Mr. Chairman, the main reason for which I have decided to bring forth this amendment is that it was shown in this house that the bill presently under discussion amending the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, while liable to do a great deal of good to many farmers who will be able to avail themselves of this measure, will also greatly prejudice the farming class, which, on account of this legislation, will lose a considerable part of their credit. The object of my amendment is to prevent this measure from being applied to debts incurred by the farmers after its adoption. I do not see why future debts should be included in this bill.
The farmer's credit is practically gone; it has been eliminated by various circumstances. First, it has been cut down since a few years, because of the lack of a market for farm products. It was also considerably imperilled by this Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, passed by the dominion parliament at its last session. I understand that under the bill that we are now discussing a board of review can compel the creditors to accept a reduction *of debts, as regards principal, and interest as well. Farmers owe presently considerable amounts and, in my estimation, we should make this legislation applicable only to present debts and not to future obligations. Undoubtedly the farmers, on account of this federal legislation, will be unable to get further credit. I cannot blame a rentier or a small money lender for refusing a loan to farmers under such conditions, because a board of review may always interfere and make him lose part of his loan or force upon him some very prejudicial arrangement.
The debts with which farms are now burdened are of enormous proportions. According to a report laid before this house there are in Canada 728,623 farm owners or tenants, 583,706 of whom own their land. There are 126,120 in the province of Quebec, 156,678 in Ontario, 37,769 in Manitoba, 90,250 in Saskatchewan, 70,751 in Alberta and 21,211 in British Columbia.
Now if we consider the total debt on farm lands, we see that these farms are mortgaged for an amount of $726,026,500. Farm lands in the province of Quebec are mortgaged for an amount of $98,121,500, and those of Ontario for an amount of $210,315,900.
The farmers of Saskatchewan have incurred debts to the amount of S196,558,300 while those of Alberta have reached a total of $120,361,100, and the farm mortgages in Manitoba, a total of $67,157,500.
Now if we examine the municipal assessment on farms in this country, we find that a total of 88,791,349,010 is reached. In Quebec, the total assessment is $2,269,148,711 and in Ontario, $3,207,396,156. We find, that the number of agriculturists is comparatively low in relation to the total population of this dominion. It is easy to realize that our country, which should be mostly agricultural, has perhaps become over-industrialized. It is apparent that the population of this country has left the farm for the great industrial centres. Probably this lack of proportion between our rural and our industrial or commercial population is the cause of most of our difficulties.
Mr. Chairman, to help the farmer, the gov-vernment has seen fit to adopt this Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Whoever thinks that this legislation is going to cost the government a great deal is wrong; in fact, the gov-vernment will have nothing to pay. The cost of this aid to a restricted number of farmers will fall back on the small rentiers, the small money lenders or on the farmers who have sold their farms. As has been stated in this house very few farmers will profit by the act.

speechtext:
Is the hon.
member for or against the act?
Ask the hon. minister's opinion.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I do not want an answer from the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) but from the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Ferland).

I do not
want the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) to question me; if he would be kind enough to listen to me, he will know whether I am for or against this law.

Could the
Postmaster General state his opinion?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Do not go
beyond your wit.

I am in
favour of extending to the farmers all the aid

Farmers' Creditors Act

possible, but before approving a bill of this importance we should study it and, if necessary, amend or modify it.
Both the act under discussion and the Canadian Farm Loan Act which has also been amended during the present session are twins, if I may say so.

They are
children of the same family who are bound to devour each other.

The Canadian Farm Loan Act puts about 90 millions of dollars at the disposal of our farming community. Don't let the farmers believe for one moment that all of them will benefit by that act, because, considering the enormous amount of farmers' debts or mortgages, as I have been showing, a relatively small number of farmers will be in a position to avail themselves of the Canadian Farm Loan Act.
The last named measure cannot be injurious to anybody, and it is a good point for it. It will be of assistance to those who will have the chance to avail themselves of its provisions, but I am quite sure it will not harm anybody. The same thing might be said of the Moratorium Act passed in the province of Quebec by the Taschereau government. One thing is sure, and that is that nobody has suffered any harm from it so far and that it has helped a great number of debtors. However, may I add, the Quebec moratorium measure has not gone far enough. Under that act, when a mortgagor is in a position to prove that he has paid his interest, whatever the interest may be, and also his taxes, except for the current year, he may avail himself of that act, but for only one year. To my mind, the act ought to go much farther and apply also to persons who are indebted in the ordinary way. There would be no inconvenience if the moratorium measure, in the province of Quebec, did not make any distinction between a mortgage and an ordinary debt, because experience had shown to me that, very often, a mortgagee will grant a delay to his debtor, whereas the ordinary creditor will have the mortgaged property sold. If I may offer a suggestion, I would say that the Moratorium Act, which I think has been wrongly criticized, might go much further and enact that a debtor who had been paying even a smaller rate of interest than was specified in his contract, say 3 or 4 per cent, could avail himself of that act.
As for the Canadian Farm Loan Act, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) is painting it' in very rosy colours. I am glad to say
[Mr. Ferland.J
that the act will give relief to a number of farmers, but it will not save the farming community in general.
The Farm Loan Act is, so to speak, a beautiful' golden chest containing a fortune of ninety million dollars. The bad side of the act-I do not know whether it can be corrected in that respect-is that the government keeps the' key of this chest filled with gold. Under this act, the commission will be able to frame regulations, approved by order in council, and to fix the basis of valuation of the land and the farm buildings. That is the key of the Farm Loan Act. The act does not rest, therefore, on fixed and definite principles destined to guide the farmer belonging to one class or another, but opens the door to arbitrary action and to the essentially variable judgments of the members and representatives of the Canadian farm loan board, who, of course, will be appointees of the dominion government. It is therefore the key-

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: It is the control key.

The control key! Were the act to be administered in the proper spirit, with breadth ol view and generosity, taking into account not only the actual value of the farms at to-day's prices, but rather their intrinsic value based on the moral character of their owners, I would say that it is capable of giving satisfactory results. Of course, the future will tell us in what spirit it will have been administered, but it is far from certain that it will not be administered, as many act3 of the present government have been, in a spirit of political partisanship.
The Farm Loan Act has been in force prior to this session's amendments. We find that, since this government assumed office, 3,330 farmers from all parts of the country have taken advantage of its provisions and have borrowed a total of 87,347,600. I see that farmers of the province of Quebec have borrowed $2,977,300 under the act, although the farm mortgages in force in that province total $98,121,500. This means that, in Quebec, as in the other provinces, the Canadian Farm Loan Act has been of practically no advantage to the community.
Will the new Farm Loan Act operate to better advantage? All we know is that a larger sum has been placed at the disposal of the farmers. However, when I consider that the amount made available under the old act has not been fully used, since, out

of $15,000,000, $7,347,600 only have been loaned over a period of four or five years, I doubt very much whether, even with this chest of 90 million dollars, the farmers will be greatly aided if the delays of the past are to recur.
Through my amendment the act would not
apply to the future liabilities of the farmers. I wonder if any man familiar with the farmers' problems may logically and reasonably oppose the suggestion I make to the house. Why on account of this act should' the farmer be unable in the future to borrow a few thousand dollars or a smaller amount? Why leave the lender open to the risks resulting from the act such as it appears in the statutes?
It is absolutely true and undeniable, I submit, that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act deals a fatal blow to agricultural credit. If it is necessary to-day on account of the extraordinary situation of the farmers, it is because they are completely ruined, because their credit is destroyed, because the farming class is in a general state of distress and because the government does not deem proper to leave them at the mercy of their creditors and, in a large number of cases open to eviction from their farms. But I submit that if this measure be necessary, it is on account of the bad policies of the government, of the high tariffs, which protected industry alone and in aiming to protect industry brought trade, industry and agriculture to the threshold of bankruptcy. At least let us not legislate in such a way as to completely destroy whatever credit the farmer may still enjoy in the future. Let us confine ourselves to the present, for before long the people may regain their former confidence and more easily recover the credit they enjoyed in the past and thereby solve their own problems under more favourable conditions. But we will not succeed, if by means of this measure we empower a board of review to reduce the amount of future debts. To my mind, the government should confine themselves to the present situation and to the winding up of their general failure in the country.
What will happen, if my amendment does not carry?
It will be carried.

The time will come when it will be impossible for any farmer to borrow money again. May I quote a few cases? In my own constituency of Joliette there are quite a number of

Farmers' Creditors Act
farmers, industrious and hard workers, who have been successful in preserving the property inherited from their ancestors and who have managed to improve the same and also raised large and fine families. During the last few weeks, I noticed-for I visit my constituency eveiy week-that the wealthier farmers, even those who have no visible debts or mortgages on their farms, are not even able to borrow any amount ranging from a thousand to two thousand dollars should they wish to help a relative or an intimate friend.
Only yesterday, one of the wealthiest farmers in the parish of St. Thomas de Joliette, called on me at my office in Joliette with the sum of seven hundred dollars as payment on account on a principal of a thousand dollars, after having requested an extension of time. I was compelled to agree to a further delay of a few days in which to raise the amount he required for the payment of a debt.
Another farmer from the parish of Ste-Elisabeth, who is free from any debts, vainly seeks to borrow a sum of a thousand dollars for a pressing need. It is unnecessary for me to mention any more such cases. Is it not a recognized fact that the farmer's credit is destroyed and completely gone? Everyone merely guesses and surmises at the causes which have ruined the farmers' credit. Honourable members sitting on the right side of Mr. Speaker are taking to task the Hon. Mr. Taschereau for having caused a moratorium act to be passed; he is accused of having destroyed the farmers' credit. However, the moratorium act in the province of Quebec does not deal at all with the capital nor the interest. On the contrary, it serves to protect those who lend money and compels the borrowers to pay their taxes, their interest and their insurance premiums, in order to secure any time extension.
On the other hand, some say that the legislation now before us is responsible for the farmers having lost their credit. In my judgment, the two main causes of this state of affairs are the selling at a loss of farm products, and in the second place, the legislation now before us. As I stated at the outset of my remarks, this legislation will prove beneficial, in particular cases, to a number of the farming community, but, as far as the farmers' credit is concerned, it will be harmful to the farmers generally. Then, would it not be wise, for the hon. members, to consider that no valid reason exists for doing anything likely to affect the farmers' credit in the future? If the farmers are so near ruination that it has become necessary to pass legislation of this kind, which directly
Farmers' Creditors Act

affects the citizens' rights and the creditors' privileges, I suibmit, on the other hand, there is no reason why it should apply to future debts. Should at any time circumstances show that such legislation has become a necessity, there would always be ample time to consider the opportunity of passing it, inasmuch as parliament meets at least once a year. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay, that my amendment be adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Joliette has submitted his amendment in French and I regret that I have not a sufficient knowledge of that language to give a literal translation of his remarks, much less to enable me to reply to him in the same tongue. As I understand it, in layman's language, he seeks by this amendment to make it clear that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act is not applicable to those obligations incurred by the farmer after the present bill is assented to. With respect to the principle that he has in mind, I am inclined to agree with him; at all events it is a fair subject of discussion, although I raise this question as to whether that amendment is designed to be of advantage to the farmer. It is an arguable question whether that is so or not. But it does seems to me that the main point is covered by the circumstance that this act will in the nature of things not be a continuing act; next session or the session following it may be repealed. It will apply only for such length of time as its usefulness is apparent. But I could hardly conceive of a case, even if this amendment were not passed, where a fresh borrowing could be the subject of adjudication under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. And when I say a fresh borrowing, I cannot conceive of an instance where a farmer, within two or three years after entering into contractual obligations, could present a set of altered circumstances that would enable him to go either before the official receiver or before the board of review.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, to do so would be
prima facie evidence of bad faith; I should say that would be a fair inference, because the obligation would be incurred under conditions which we have every reason to assume will not be worse. The probabilities are that they will be better, and if the farmer finds himself in two or three years' time in the position suggested, assuming that the Fanners' Creditors Arrangement Act were in operation for that length of time,

then I should say the inference was that he had not disclosed circumstances which he ought to have made known in incurring the obligation in the first instance. That however is a matter that need not be laboured. If it is the sense of the committee that an amendment of this kind should be inserted, so far as I am concerned I have no objection.
Will the chairman please read the amendment in English.

Mr. Ferland moves that the following clause be added:
6. Section 18 of the said act is amended by adding to section 18 the following clause:
"The present act shall not apply to future debts which farmers contract after the day on which the act as amended comes into force.

With reference to the
remarks made by the Minister of Finance, I might point out to him that this amendment covers future debts. One of the points of this legislation that is worrying me is that if a farmer acting in the best of faith goes to his merchant desirous of buying $50 or $75 worth of goods, there is to-day no basis whereby the merchant can give him credit, because if he does, to-morrow or six months hence the farmer can go under the debt adjustment act and there is therefore no basis at all for credit. I suggest to the minister that this is an amendment that should receive the concurrence of the committee. I believe it is designed to help out those whom we are trying to help by the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and I really think it should be given very serious consideration before the government refuses it.

The hon. member for
Vancouver-Burrard refers to the act as if anybody can invoke its protection to suit his whim. I do not think the act was designed for that purpose or has been administered to that end. It is merely a bankruptcy act for the farmer without the cost or the delay which characterize bankruptcy proceedings. When the hon. gentleman speaks of a farmer who might go to his grocer and might not receive credit because he could have recourse to this act, my hon. friend is entirely overlooking the fact that every hon. member is in exactly the same position. Everv citizen of Canada, the farmers excepted, has access to the Bankruptcy Act. I do not think the hon. gentleman wishes to insinuate that the farming class is dishonest or any more dishonest than any other class and would attempt to evade its responsibilities by appealing to the protection of this

Farmers' Creditors Act
act. After all the act is applied by people who are honest, competent and able, and a person may not merely go to the official receiver and say: I want the protection of this act. No; he has to go with a statement of his assets and liabilities. After they have been examined and scrutinized most carefully, then the official receiver calls in all the creditors, and after a lengthy debate in which all parties are heard, it is decided whether there is any reason to apply the act. I can assure the hon. gentleman that so far the fears which he expresses have not found their way into the experience of anybody who has had to do with the act.
The hon. member for Joliette went rather far afield. He told the committee that the farmer was in a difficult situation because of the activities of this government.
Lack of activity.

He went on to say how hard was the position of the farmer because he had lost his market. I do not wish to traverse ground which has been gone over so often. I do not think anybody who has graduated from the kindergarten of politics will tarry very long with that statement. Everybody knows not a single trade barrier has been raised against this country since the present government came into office. I am not attempting for a moment to insinuate or suggest-and even if I so wished, this is not the time to do it-that the attitude of the late government may have had something to do with the attitude of other countries toward us, but we must all admit that no market in which agricultural products have been sold has been closed to this country during this government's tenure of office. In faot our markets for agricultural products have been enlarged and vastly enlarged since the government came into office, and hon. gentlemen know that as well as I do.
Forty cents for butter.

That is about as near as my hon. friend can come to understanding. what a market means. I can tell the hon. gentleman, since he refers to butter, that the last year his party was in office 40,000.000 pounds of foreign butter were brought into this country, whereas now the Canadian farmer supplies our market.
Let us take up for a moment the second suggestion olf the hon. member for Joliette. He has suggested that the farmer has lost his credit and told us that he lost it some time ago. Then he attributes this loss of credit to the passing of this act a few months
ago. Then he asks that this act for which he voted should ibe amended in order to prevent loss of credit by the farmer. I fail to fallow his logic. The farmer may not have as much credit as he wishes, but this act is devised to rehabilitate the farmer; I think the farmer will be the first to acknowledge that the act has not caused loss of credit as the hon. member for Joliette has suggested. I do not think anybody is under the delusion that this act has brought loss to anybody. It was designed to do away with the confusion which has resulted from losses already made and to clear away the debris and give the farmer a chance to begin over again, to give him the opportunity that every other class of our population has by recourse to the Bankruptcy Act.
I have no particular objection to the amendment, but I think it is unfair to the farming class. Why should the farmer who has met with some great disaster, some great calamity, be shackled to the ball and chain of debt for the rest of his life while others are able to shake themselves free? Hon. GROTE STIRLING (Acting Minister of Fisheries) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act to provide that the governor in council may from time to time prescribe a tariff of fees that shall be charged for the inspection of canned fish and shell fish.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.
Explain.

speakeroldname: Hon. GROTE STIRLING (Acting Minister ol Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the sole purpose of the amendment is to regularize what has been done in recent years with regard to fees. Perhaps I should read the explanatory note in the bill.
Section 4 of the Meat and Canned Foods Act authorizes the governor in council to make such orders and regulations not inconsistent with the provisions of the act as seem necessary for carrying out its provisions. Section 18 of the aot authorizes regulations for the inspection of canned fish and shell fish. By order in council of April 4, 1932, regulations for the inspection of all canned salmon packed in British Columbia were adopted. Section 20 of these regulations provides for a fee for inspection at the rate of one per cent per case. The fee is a reasonable one, and at present covers only the cost of inspection. No difficulty has arisen in the collection of the fee, but there is room for doubt as to whether, in the absence of a specific statutory provision, it can be legally required. As fees paid in the past are not recoverable, the amendment does not need to be retroactive.
There is no question but that the act gives the minister power to grant licences, but the question has been raised as to whether or not the governor in council by regulation may prescribe a tariff of fees. It is to insert such provision in the act that the amendment is suggested.
I believe the last remarks of the minister apply to the next resolution on the order paper. We are not dealing with the resolution concerning the tariff on licences.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We are dealing with the amendment to the Meat and Canned Foods Aot.

Yes. I believe in some
measure I am subject to blame, or to credit, for this resolution being brought forward, and for the legislation which may be based upon it. In 1932, when the government introduced a most elaborate system of inspection of canned salmon, a system far different from that which had previously existed, I protested not against the principle of the inspection of fish, which was very necessary, but against the method by which the inspectors were selected, and also the way in which the charges were made.
That my objections had some weight is borne out by the fact that only a few months later it was necessary substantially to amend the regulations, and the same procedure was followed in the next year. One of my objections was that I thought it was not fair or just, and hardly legal, that the canners should be picked out and compelled by regulation to pay what really amounts to a very large sum for the inspection of their product. I shall deal with that point later on. At the end of the session I took up the question of the legality of the measure, and stressed the argument that the government had no authority to impose substantial taxation-because that is what it amounts to-on any one industry, by means of regulations made in pursuance of a modest and obscure section in an act giving the government power to make regulations for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the act. Certainly the government has power to make regulations for carrying out the provisions of the act, but they have no power by regulation to make a totally different law. They might as well put something about customs duties in it- in fact in one instance I believe they did- or make a regulation compelling people to be cremated.
That my views have prevailed is evidenced by the fact that the present legislation is before us. I wish to take advantage of the opportunity now afforded to deal with the matter of charges levied against the canners. The Meat and Canned Foods Act is general, and the provisions are such that they apply to the inspection of any product. The act provides that commodities shall not be sold unless they are inspected, and that they must be sound, wholesome, and so on. These are sections of a general character. Then regulations are made dealing with products such as vegetables and preserved fruits, and there are further regulations dealing with fish.
I notice that in the canned foods act the section dealing with the inspection of pre-
Meat and Canned Foods Act

served fruits and vegetables lays down that the inspector shall be appointed by the government and, inferentially at least, be paid by the government, and we do know that he is paid by the government. The act calls attention to various things. The inspector has tc visit the cannery, notice the sanitary arrange ments and so on, see that the fruit shall bt wholesome, but his inspection is devotee largely to this point:	He has to go there
and see the operations of the cannery, set that the conditions are cleanly and that the fruit is wholesome, that any dyes that are used are sound and wholesome, and then he gives a certificate. Any stuff that is exported carries this certificate by the inspector:
I have examined . .. containers or packages-
I ask the house to notice that; he can examine as many or as few packages as he likes.
I have examined .... containers or packages taken from various parts of the shipment, and judging by the markings thereon I would consider said packages and containers were marked to meet the requirements of the "Meat and Canned Foods Act," and the regulations made thereunder.
That is quite all right, but is that the principle embodied in this resolution? Not at all. In the case of meat and butter and vegetables and so on, the inspector is paid by the government. He goes and inspects a carcass of beef. He does not have to cut off a chunk of the beef to inspect it. He can see its condition. But in the inspection of canned goods it is quite different. But there is no provision in the act where it deals with fruit saying how many cans the inspector must open. The whole purpose of the regulations and of the act is that the inspection shall be of the stuff while it is being manufactured. The inspector does not sit down and wait until the stuff is all put in cans and then come around, as they do with fish, and confiscate a comparatively large proportion of the product. The inspector simply bases his decision in the case of fruit on what he sees in his inspection of the cannery, and if necessary he has the power to take one or two cans and open them, but there is no compulsion on him at all to open any particular number of cans, nor is there in the case of meats packed in the packing houses.
But let us look at the picture that is now proposed, and that has been in force three years in connection with the unhappy salmon canners. First of all the canner has to pay for everything, and he has to pay for the inspection of his product in two ways. He pays through the nose. He begins by paying one cent a case. Now the ordinary
[Mr. NeillJ
large canning company will pack 100,000 cases of salmon, and at one cent a case that means a charge of SI,000. They call it an inspection fee. That sounds very nice, just an inspection fee. It sounds like something you carry around in your pocket, but it is $1,000. Does the beef man and the fruit man have to pay $1,000 for his inspection? Not a bit. Then why should the cannery man?
There is a further tax, and a quite substantial one. The last order in council- they have been varied a good many times- prescribes, I don't know why-it is not the case with fruit and other stuff-exactly how many cases are to be drawn out of a given number, and one tin has to be taken out of each one of those cases and opened, and of course it is lost. Who pays for that? Again it is the canner. But the man with a side of beef does not have to lose anything on his beef if it passes muster. But the poor canner loses every tin that is opened. In the case of other produce the inspector might open certain tins and then be inclined to say, "This shipment was all put up on the same day or the same two or three days, and I assume the rest is of the same quality." But he cannot do that when he inspects canned fish. It is fixed by the regulations that he must open so many cases and take out of each case one tin, and of course each tin opened is lost, and that is all done at the expense of the canner. One would suppose that it would be enough to make him lose that without making him pay in addition $1,000 for the privilege of that inspection.
Then there are different classes, and you do not have to draw so many cases in the higher classes. You have to take eighteen cases out of every hundred cases and draw one tin out of each of those eighteen. That will carry you up to 500 cases. I notice that as usual the greater expense is put on the small man. The small man would probably not draw out more than 100 cases of salmon at a time but eighteen cases have to be drawn out of the 100 cases,, and as I say every one of those cases has to be opened and a tin taken out. Now, in the case of a pack of 100,000 cases, eighteen cases out of 100 would mean taking out 18,000 cases, out of each of which a tin has to be taken. That means that another tin has to be put in and the case nailed up again. That costs something. If you take the other extreme of the class, which runs from 101 to 500, if you get 500 cases inspected at one time they have to take only the same number, eighteen out of 500. That would be 3,600 cases which would have to be opened

Meat and Canned Foods Act
and a tin taken out of each. Now as to costs -I am speaking of the more valuable grade of sockeye salmon. The loss on these tins would amount to 375 cases or something like $5,600 through the loss of the tins opened, in the case of the lower regulation, and the inspector has no discretion at all. He has got to open a case and take out that tin and throw the contents away, one tin out of each case. On the other hand, under the higher regulation, he would not have to take out so many and the loss would amount to only $1,125. But that is in addition to the $1,000, at the rate of one cent a case, that the canner has already paid for the inspection fee.
The whole thing is wrong. This is not the time for me to make some comments on the system of appointing these inspectors. Perhaps I will have an opportunity later. But the whole system is wrong and my strictures upon it three years ago have been wholly justified. But that is not the point at the moment.
The inspectors are appointed, by the way, on the recommendation of the people who have to pay them and whose stuff they are going to inspect, men who are in the same business as the canners themselves and competing with them. They are appointed by the government, we will suppose, and they are paid by the canner. It involves a heavy expense, unparalleled in the inspection of any other article. Does the cheese man have to pay the equivalent of one cent a case for every cheese that is inspected? Not at all. The government carries the expense of that as a contribution towards the advantages accruing from a higher grade product. Why should the salmon canner, who is running in very hard luck these days on account of competition and so on, be penalized because the government have seen fit, quite properly, to have his stuff inspected. If we make the cannery man pay for the inspection of his stuff, I hope the others will be made to pay for the inspection of their stuff.
As I say, there is a double charge to the canner. First of all he has to pay one oent a case, and that is quite a substantial tax; it is not a fee at all. Then he has to lose every tin that is opened, and the inspector is compelled to open these tins and throw them away It is a heavy expense for the canner. Surely that should be a sufficient imposition upon him without having to pay one cent a case as well. I submit to the minister that before he brings down the bill he might take that feature into consideration.
I do not think there is anything further that I can add. There is the case, and as far as I know it cannot be combatted. It is not fair for the industry, and I do not think it has a parallel in any other industry in Canada to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member has taken the opportunity of levelling some pretty considerable criticism in detail at the resolution stage. That was my only idea in bringing it on at this stage. However, if he wishes to report the resolution I have no objection.

speechtext: As I have already explained, this is an extremely simple amendment empowering the governor in council from time to time to prescribe a tariff of fees. speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have no objection to its going to that committee.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I cannot understand what object there is in sending it to the fisheries committee. It is a bill to permit the charging of fees, and has nothing to do
Fisheries Act

with the general provisions of the act. We should like to oblige the hon. gentleman, if there were any object in sending it to the fisheries committee, but when the bill is brought down he will perhaps again raise his point.

If it is not illegal it is highly unfair to charge them at all, and that is why I suggested that it would be better to have it discussed in the fisheries committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence

Perhaps I might read the explanatory note of this bill:
Section 34 of the Fisheries Act gives the governor in council authority, amongst other things, "to forbid fishing except under authority of leases or licences." There was similar authority in previous Fisheries Acts since confederation. Under it, regulations have all along been adopted by order in council requiring, for idministrative purposes, that licences must be jbtained before engaging in certain kinds of fishing, and specifying fees for such licences. While no difficulty has arisen in the collection of the fees, there is room for doubt as to whether in the absence of specific statutory provision, fees can legally be required. As fees paid in the past are not recoverable, the amendment does not need to be retroactive.
The exception referred to is section 9, subsection 4, of the act, which provides a fee of fifty dollars for hunting whales in Hudson bay.
As a lease implies a rental the charge would not come within the category of a fee.

It is intended to correct that situation.
