speechtext: To provide for expenses connected with the administration of Indian Affairs, including salaries, supplies, relief, medical attendance, hospitalization, dwellings, agricultural activities, surveys, roads, bridges, irrigation, dyking, education, et cetera, and a grant of $100,000 approved by parliament in session of 1926-27, $4,260,000.

Could the minister give us some explanation of how supplies are purchased for the requirements of the Indians on the various reserves, such as hardware, lumber, groceries and general supplies of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Supplies are purchased in two ways. First, we contract at the beginning of the season for certain general supplies for the use of Indians throughout Canada. In other words the experience of years has taught us how we may anticipate the demands. There are always a certain number of destitute and aged Indians and we are also under treaty obligation with certain bands to provide them with certain supplies. We anticipate these requirements and contract for them early in the season, obtaining prices on tender forms. These supplies are then purchased and shipped at the most advantageous time to different reserves. To certain reserves it is necessary to ship goods early in the season, as they have to go in by dog train, or at other times by boat. If by dog train we endeavour to ship them early in the season in order to make use of the ice and thereby secure a more advantageous route. Needless to say we are not able to anticipate all our requirements, so it is necessary to supplement those contract supplies by purchases later in the year. These purchases are made by the various agents in charge of the reserves, or other officers whose services we utilize. These supplies are bought to the best advantage either locally or from wholesale merchants, in whatever manner seems best to the agent or the department.

That is just the point I wanted to bring out. When extra supplies are required during the year I understand they are purchased by the Indian agent, as the minister says, to the best advantage. Does he call for tenders or competitive bias from all those dealing in the particular lines of goods required, or has he the privilege of
Supply-Indian Affairs

going to a particular store and ordering the supplies without giving others a chance to bid?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It depends to a certain extent on the amount of Ithe purchase. If it is an appreciable amount, tenders are requested and the order placed with the lowest tenderer. Certain supplies of small amount the agent purchases to the best advantage without calling for tenders.
Suppose a dozen cook stoves are required, would that be an order of sufficient size to make it necessary for the agent to advertise for tenders and accept the lowest satisfactory tender?

speechtext:

Yes.

I wonder if the
minister would be kind enough to inform me what classes of Indians are entitled to these

Supply-Indian Affairs
supplies. I should like to know also if the Indian agents furnish only actual supplies or if they provide money as well. Further I should like1 to know if the half-breeds are entitled to this help as well as other Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Some Indians receive supplies under the various treaties which have been entered into between the Indians in question and the crown. Others are supplied because they are destitute or ill. Others are looked after because, like other people, through no fault of their own they have been unable to provide a livelihood for themselves. The only Indians who receive money are those who receive it under treaty or from the interest funds of the band to which they belong, provided they have a capital sum to their credit with the dominion government.

I had in mind some special cases in the province of Quebec. speechtext: No, supplies are not furnished to half-breeds. Only the Indians who come within the definition of the Indian Act are supplied.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The drug supplies are furnished to the medical officers on the reserves, or in some cases to missionaries or others where we have* no medical men. The department obtains these supplies from the Department of Pensions and National Health in Ottawa, and they are forwarded to the various agencies throughout Canada. In addition to that, of course, medical men who are called upon to provide medical attention to these Indians may write prescriptions for sick Indians and have them filled at local drug stores, or if necessary they may purchase supplies locally if those furnished by the department are not sufficient or are not of the kind required in any particular case.

A year ago I took a few moments of the time of the committee to present the case of the Six Nations Indians on the reserve at Tuscarora, in the county of Brant. I pointed out that, these Indians always having been wards of the government, like other Indians of the dominion, funds belonging to the Six Nations Indians and in possession of the government of the day were improperly diverted, in breach of trust, for the purpose of building or helping to build a canal known as the Grand River navigation canal. The moneys then misappropriated, as I say, together with interest and other moneys advanced from time to time by the government of the day, amount in the aggregate to over $1,000,000. I am told that the contention of the Department of Justice is that this matter is outlawed or that the present government of Canada is not responsible for what was done by a previous government of this part of Canada. I cannot see it in that way. I do not wish to repeat the arguments I advanced last year, but I shall call to the attention of
Supply-Indian Affairs

the committee the concluding words of the reply the minister was good enough to make following my observations. He said, as reported at page 2416 of Hansard for 1934:
I wish to assure him-
And the minister was referring to me.
-that so far as I am concerned, within the limits imposed upon me I shall endeavour to see that justice is done.
I find nothing in the estimates to cover the expenditure I have suggested. I have not asked for an appropriation of a million dollars. I recognize that there is some merit-not very much-but some merit in the contention that the present government is not responsible for this expropriation of funds. I wish again to suggest to the minister that a substantial sum be placed in the supplementary estimates for the purpose I have suggested. Such an expenditure would go a long way towards wiping out the dissatisfaction which exists among the Indians who were wrongfully deprived of money. I would not expect the amount to be charged this year against income; it is really a capital expenditure which should be charged against capital. The expenditure should not interfere with the financial position of the government, so far as the revenues for the year are concerned. Again I ask the minister to consider the matter and if possible to place a substantial sum in the supplementary estimates for the purpose I have indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member drew this matter to my attention last year when the estimates for the Department of Indian Affairs were under discussion. He has correctly quoted my remarks upon that occasion. I believe at this time I have nothing to add to my former observations, but I assure the hon. member that I shall be pleased to take the matter into the fullest consideration when supplementary estimates are being considered.

Mr. Chairman, there are some circumstances I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. Last year I communicated with him in connection with a man named Edouard Moreau who lived at Ste. Agnes de Charlevoix, a village behind Murray Bay. In a letter addressed to me under date of March 16, 1934, the minister said the man in question should present himself to the nearest Indian agency and apply for relief, in which case he would receive the necessary attention. Ini this instance the nearest Indian reserve is at Bersimis, and the next two are at Seven Islands and Mingan. At those points are located the three large Indian reserves in my constituency, and all are at 
great distances from this man's home. Would the minister indicate what could be done in circumstances such as these? Then, at a place called Les Escoumains in the county of Saguenay, there is a small settlement of Indians. They have their quarters near the village. Apparently they do not belong to any of the reserves, but live on their own lands and are educating their children. I believe the children of these Indians go to the village school. It would seem however that they do not receive any grant. The next reserve is at Bersimis, a point about sixty or seventy miles away, and these people would not be in a position to travel that far. In such circumstances w'hat may they expect from the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the event of the Indians in question being located at points distant from Indian reserves they would be required to write to the department at Ottawa or, if they were unable to do so, have someone write for them bringing their condition to the attention of the department. In such circumstances proper arrangements would be made for their relief, in the event of their being in need. As I said a few moments ago, in some of the remoter areas where we find difficulty in having agents operate we have utilized the services of the missionaries. In other cases where there are only a few Indians at one point, so few in fact that it would not be proper to have an agent to look after them, the Indians or some persons on their behalf would write to the department, and in the event of its being shown that they were in need of food, fuel, clothing, or medical services, proper steps would be taken by ihe department.

What amount is provided under the vote for the education of the Indians? Further, how long have we been educating Indians, and are those educational facilities supplied as a result of treaty arrangements? Is there any compulsion in matters of education?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the total amount allotted for education in the year 1935-36 is SI,846,000. Where school facilities are furnished the Indian children are supposed to attend school. In other words compulsory attendance applies.
Possibly the minister did not hear all my question. I asked how long we had been educating Indians, and to what extent the education had been given.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the first instance education began through the efforts of various

Supply-Indian Affairs
missionary societies in Canada, that is to say through the efforts of the Roman Catholic church and the Anglican church, which were followed in the work by the Methodist church *-now part of the United church-and the Presbyterian church. These religious bodies sent missionaries among the Indians, and in order better to explain their doctrines they attempted the education of Indian children. Many schools were organized throughout the dominion which, in the first instance, were carried on as the sole charge of the various churches. Then later-I cannot give the exact date- these churches made appeals to the dominion government for grants to assist them in the education of the Indian children. As a result the dominion government has for a number of years provided per capita grants to the various schools conducted by different church denominations. Again at a later point day schools were built on the reserves where the Idians had more or less settled habits. In that way the Indian child of to-day is obtaining or should obtain a public school education.
Could the minister g:ve any information to indicate whether or not the education given to the Indian children has been of any real benefit, and in what way the results ars shown?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a question to which one could scarcely be expected to give a dogmatic or explicit answer, nor could one prove his answer were he called upon to do so. I have discussed the point with those in authority, and with people who are deeply interested in the education of the Indians in Canada, and they are unanimously of the opinion that the education has been beneficial to the Indians, and particularly to those who are living in what might be described as the more civilized sections of Canada. Where children living in the more remote districts are taken to points hundreds of miles distant and placed in residential schools, going back after their school term to the wilder parts of Canada to make their living by the chase, the results are not so satisfactory as in the case of those living in the more settled parts of the dominion. I am told by the church authorities particularly that on the part of children of former pupils of the residential schools there is a noticeable difference in the ability to absorb education; that is to say, the second generation attending school show more evidence of benefit than the first.

May I ask the minister
if there is any government inspection of assisted schools?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the Indian schools are inspected by the various public school inspectors throught Canada with the exception of British Columbia and New Brunswick in which provinces the department employ its own inspectors.

assistance for needy Indians on the reserves, is there any definite schedule of relief?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, there is no definite
schedule, because as the hon. member will realize the conditions on all the reserves are not the same, and the supplies that it may be necessary to furnish to the Indians in Ontario might vary considerably from the supplies necessary in British Columbia. I note that in the estimate for Indian Affairs $320,000 is asked in excess of last year's amount, and I also note that the estimate covers bridges, roads and other necessary works. May I ask the minister whether there is any appropriation for the upkeep and repairs of bridges on the road across the Indian reserve in the township of Doncaster, county of Terrebonne, province of Quebec? During the last two years correspondence has been exchanged with the department and the reply has been that there was no appropriation. As there is $320,000 more for next year, will the Department of Indian Affairs during the winter take care of the road crossing that Indian reserve and have the bridges repaired so that there will be no further accidents?-because some took place last year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is in the estimates no appropriation for work on the road in question.

This is a public road about fourteen miles in length. It was built more than twenty years ago, and seven or eight years ago an agreement was made between the provincial government and the Department of Indian Affairs whereby each was to spend about $9,000, so that $18,000 was spent between the two governments. That was to repair and build bridges on the road from the parish of Ste. Lucie through the parish of La Merci in the county of Montcalm. The road has been in fairly good condition for six or seven years. Since this government has been in power, it has been very difficult to have the road kept in good repair and accidents

have taken place. I think some action has been taken against the government. It was claimed by the department that the road was not a public one, but it is a question whether a road that has been built and maintained and on which bridges have been constructed in conjunction with the provincial government, is a public one or not.
There was also a reply given by the department stating that the road into the parish of La Merci in the county of Montcalm had not been repaired. That was used as an argument by the department for not spending any more money on that road. But last year the provincial government spent the necessary amount of money to put its part of the road right through for about sixteen miles into perfect condition. The last reply we had from the Department of Indian Affairs was that the road was to be closed and signs were to be put at each end of it stating that it was not a public road and that the public using it did so on their own responsibility. I think that is a very bad step to take. The road to my personal knowledge has been open to the public for the past twenty years, and I think the necessary appropriation should be made and the road given proper attention. It is divided into three sections; one into the county of Montcalm in the parish of La Merci; a section of ten miles into the Indian reserve, and then about four or five miles into the parish of Ste. Lucie in the county of Terrebonne. Therefore each of the three parties is bound to keep its own sections in order that the public may not suffer from having a very bad road, especially in the winter when the road is blocked by snow. I am asking the minister to give his attention to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As the hon. member has stated, there has been certain correspondence about the road in question. I am informed by officers of the department that there is only one Indian family living on the reserve. While I believe it is true, as the hon member has stated, that this road is a public one, that is, it serves the people surrounding the reserve, allowing them to travel from one place to another, I can only repeat what I said a moment ago: no appropriation has been made in the estimates for the road in question, I shall be pleased, however, as requested by the hon. member, to give the matter my attention.
I thank the minister.

The minister a few minutes ago said that the Indian population of this country was from 112,000 to 115,000. Does

Supply-Indian Affairs
that comprise those who are wards of the government unemancipated, or all the Indians in the country, those emancipated and otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Those who are classed as Indians as defined by the act; that is to say, those who have become enfranchised are not classified as Indians after that action has been taken.
Indians who are wards of the government live on reserves in different parts of the country. Do I understand that missionary supervision is provided for all those reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That depends on the missionary zeal of the various churches. I may say though that in practically every part of Canada the Indians are receiving religious instruction from various denominations. It may be that in some of the remoter parts of Canada they are not receiving religious instruction. If there are such I am not aware of it, because the department is continually receiving letters from the various denominations from every part of Canada. Prom my personal knowledge of the last four or five years I think it can be generally stated that the Indians throughout Canada are receiving religious instruction.

That is they are attached to various Christian denominations, as I understand. Has the government anything to do with the allocation of those Indians to the various denominations? Do they settle which are to be Roman Catholics and which are to be continuing Presbyterians or United Church and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Indian exercises
freedom of choice the same as the white man. He may select his own church.
But he has not the freedom of exercising the franchise while he is a ward of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Only when he becomes enfranchised.

A little while ago the minister informed the committee that the expenditures in respect to schools on the Blackfoot reserve in eastern Alberta were $149 per head. Are there any other expenses in connection with those two schools? If so, what are they?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I find that the sum of $200 is allocated for a windmill at the Old Sun's school and $1,400 to be used for the erection of a henhouse, pig pen, silo, and for paint for the buildings and barns.
These expenditures are in respect to the Old Sun's school?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Those I have just mentioned, yes.
Are there any for the Cluny school?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no specific item in the estimates for the school in question, although we have a general item on which we draw for the purposes of general repairs and such things.
Have any requests been received during the year for additional expenditures in respect of the Cluny school?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I am informed that there have been.
What were they?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that last year there was a fire in the school, and that some $1,500 was spent during the fiscal year
1934-35 on repairs, and that certain other repairs have been requested, which are being taken care of out of the general item that I mentioned a moment ago.
May I be assured by the minister that they will be taken care of?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All necessary repairs will be attended to.

We shall see
next year.
How many Indians were enfranchised, if any, in the district of Charle-voix-Saguenay?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: None.
Could the minister tell us if the Indian fund, which belongs to the Indians and out of which they are supposed to receive grants, has been depleted or increased within the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At the beginning of the fiscal year the total to the credit of the Indian trust fund was $13,580,007.18. At the end of the fiscal year it stood at 813,602,564.74-a slight increase.
Where did the increase come from-interest earned, or new sources of revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would come from
general sources such as sales of timber, pos-
Supply-Indian Affairs

sibly sales of land; and in addition it might be augmented by the interest credited by the dominion government at the rate of five per cent per annum, which may not all be used or distributed among the Indians.

Were there any sales
of land or timber on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can assure the hon.
member that there was no sale of land. I would have to ascertain if there were sales of timber or any other resources.

Has the department
received any requests for leases of timber limits of which I spoke a few minutes ago in the Bersimis district?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The officials have made
a note of that request. I have not the information now but I shall be glad to get it.

May these Indians leave
the reserves and become regular citizens of Canada with voting privileges?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are free agents,
that is to say there is no law which compels an Indian to remain on the reserve. He may leave the reserve and still be classed as an Indian, or he may apply to the department to become enfranchised, which action is taken if after investigation it is thought proper to do so. If he becomes enfranchised then he has the privilege of voting.

Are the Indians showing a
tendency to leave the reserves and become assimilated with the rest of the population, and if so to what extent?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the eleven months of
the present fiscal year thirty-one have been enfranchised. Adding the twenty-seven dependents makes a total of fifty-eight enfranchised during those eleven months.
Is the Indian population on the reserves increasing or decreasing, or does it remain stationary?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Generally the number of Indians is increasing, with possibly very few exceptions in certain reserves. The Indian population is increasing at about the rate of one thousand a year.

As the minister
is aware, the Indian department have been putting up certain parcels of Indian lands for sale by auction from time to time and by arrangement with the Indians their wards. During the abounding years of 1926, 1927, 1928, when land prices were very buoyant

a quantity of such land between File Hills Indian agency and the town of Hubbard on the Black Bear reserve was sold to white settlers, who now find great difficulty in paying either the interest or the principal. It has occurred to me that possibly these settlers might have the benefit of the legislation that is available to those who purchased land from other vendors such as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Hudson's Bay Company and many private vendors, and even from the Indian department themselves. These lands now are priced very much lower than they were in those earlier years, and I was wondering if anything could be done with respect to the principal owing on these lands and also in regard to the interest, which I think is six per cent. These payments are being defaulted. As my hon. friend knows, crops have not been too good and prices for all farm products have been simply terrible. Has any particular policy been adopted by the department that would give these settlers the opportunity of rearrangement that other settlers may enjoy who bought from vendors other than the Department of Indian Affairs?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has raised a question which has given the department and mysellf a great deal of concern. As he has stated these lands were sold to white settlers, but in the first instance they could be sold only after a proper surrender had been given by the Indian owners. In consenting to the surrender the Indians themselves laid down the terms and conditions under which they were prepared to surrender ithedr rights in the lands; consequently the crown acts as a trustee for the Indians in those sales. I take it that of itself the department has no power to vary the terms laid down by the Indians in regard to the surrender, but last session parliament in its wisdom passed a measure known as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, of which the farmers are availing themselves to a great extent. Settlers who purchased Indian land, I have been informed, are in the same position as other settlers who purchased land from white people or from companies. Therefore the purchaser of Indian land has the same recourse open to him that is open to other settlers throughout Canada.

That would seem to be quite satisfactory, provided that the same machinery is available in each case. I suppose the same courts will deal with both cases, that the same facilities will be available and that the possibility of reducing the rate

Supply-Indian Affairs
of interest will be the same in every case. I realize that the government is acting as the guardian of the Indians and that these sales have 'been made under agreement as to price, but there is no reason why the Indian would not be as reasonable as any other person. At the present time he is agreeing to sell similar land at a much lower price, and I think if the matter were presented to him as a creditor, like other creditors, he would possibly agree to a lower price which would correspond with the prices being received under the sales taking place at the present time, as well as a lower rate oof interest. I can see no di. .culty in that. The Indian may say a bargain is a bargain, and of course that is so, but in the years from 1927 to 1929 many bargains were made that it is simply impossible to carry out. Many of these settlers have put their all into the improvement of these lands. They have erected houses. A good many of them of course are log bouses, nevertheless it has taken a good deal of labour to put them up, together with the necessary outbuildings. This is largely wooded land, and a great deal of clearing has taken place. These settlers have every dollar they own invested in their land, and they simply cannot pay those high prices. My hon. friend is a reasonable man; he understands the conditions which exist among both the white settlers and the Indians. I do not think he would find very much difficulty in making such rearrangements as I have mentioned. But if these settlers can take advantage of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and possibly secure a reduction of their debt if the circumstances warrant it, all would seem to be well. Can the minister see anything that would make it difficult or impossible to achieve this result? I think the difficulty largely disappears if these settlers are put in the same category as other purchasers of land from vendors other than the government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
To answer the first question of my hon. friend I would say that I do see some difficulty in asking the Indians voluntarily to make settlements with those who purchased the lands in question. I think the hon. member will realize that each case must be dealt with on its merits, just the same as though the settler had purchased the land from a white person or a company. All cases are not the same. Some purchasers may have almost paid for their land in full; they may have kept uip their interest payments, while others may have allowed their interest to accumulate. There will not be two cases exactly alike; each case would have to be considered by the Indians on its merits. If
it were merely a question of reducing the price of the land or of reducing the interest, a matter on which a general judgment could be given, that might be accomplished, but certainly these cases will not be all alike. Each case will be like a matter coming before a judge and jury; it will have to be decided on its merits. That is why I think the second alternative would be much better, namely that the purchasers of Indian land avail themselves of the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, just as is done by the purchasers of land from others than Indians.

I think that is
reasonable. If there is a good settler on a piece of good easily cleared land, a man who has been making his payments, of course the assumption is that he will be able to make the rest of the payments. On the other hand another settler, due to different causes, may have gone behind; he may have made no payments, or very few. I do not know which of these men would get the better treatment. I could imagine that the official receiver might consider the man who was pretty well paid up should receive the better adjustment, because he would have the best chance of eventually paying whatever figure is arrived at. On the other hand sometimes a man gets away behind through no fault of his own, and there may be a disposition to be a little hard on him. I recognize that the merits or demerits of each case must in the main be the basis of the arrangement. I do not know that I can take any exception to that, but I would urge the minister to facilitate these arrangements in every possible way. I have seen some of the correspondence between the department and some of these purchasers of land. Sometimes, you know, when you read an official letter in black and white it sounds very harsh and exacting. The settlers are supposed to come through with their payments, but they have nothing to come through with. I hope that at least some nicer official letters will be sent to them holding out some hope of adjustment downwards, because they are now hanging on by their eyelashes and toe-nails just wondering what is going to happen next. ' Here is a government exercising supervision over this matter, and teaching ethics in business to other people, although it would seem they are not practising very nice ethics themselves. That is the way they reason. Of course, we will have to wait until we see how this matter turns out in practice, but if the same privileges were freely given these settlers as are .given to
Supply

Indian Affairs

others I believe the difficulty would be removed. I do not believe the Indians themselves will throw anything in the way of a rearranged valuation of such lands. I have found that if Indians believe other people are playing on the up and, up they also will play on the up and up. The Indian boys who are farming on the same reserve also have difficulty in making ends meet, and have no doubt little trouble would be experienced in bringing about any compromise which may be ne-' cessary to meet the exigencies of the situation in general and each case in particular. I thank the minister for his interpretation of the position, and we will now have to await events. I hope the minister, as Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, will make public his interpretation, and the interpretation of the Minister of Finance on the same subject.

Is there any particular
disease from which the Indians on reservations suffer? I understand that in olden days many Indians suffered from tuberculosis. Could the minister tell us about their health in these days, when new treatments are being adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When the Indian first
came in contact with the white man and contracted the white man's diseases he was found to be extremely susceptible to them, and once having contracted them the mortality rate was very high. Through the years, however, the Indian has developed resistance to the diseases common to the white man, and that while tuberculosis and certain other ailments are prevalent among them, we are assured by our officials who have charge of the health of Indians that there is a marked improvement in their general health.

I should like to learn from the minister how much of the S4,260,000 is spent in the province of Quebec, in Ontario and in the other provinces. Following that I should like him to tell me how much is being spent at the Caughnawaga reserve in the county of Laprairie?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The amount is divided
among the various provinces as follows:
Prince Edward Island	 $ 10,110
Nova Scotia	 143,234
New Brunswick	 110,464
Quebec	 379,931
Ontario	 774.969
Manitoba	 417,930
Saskatchewan	 599,843
Alberta	 564.791
British Columbia	 920,888
Northwest Territories	 128,521
Yukon	 41,160

Could the minister tell
what amount is to be spent at the reserva-

tion at Caughnawaga, and what proportions will be spent for irrigation, dwellings, agricultural activities, dyking and education?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
For the Caughnawaga
reservation we have estimated expenditures as follows:
Administration	 $ 3,465
Medical services	 11,650
Relief	 40,000
Roads, drainage, bridges and	so on	1,800
Nothing for bridges.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the last item is for
drainage, roads, bridges and other expenditures.

But there is nothing for
bridges.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it is included in the $1,800.

May I tell the minister
that at that point there is no bridge to be built or maintained and that for that reason I conclude no money will be spent for bridges.

They
burned their bridges.

Yes, as the hon. member
for Bow River has said, I suppose they have burned their bridges. In previous sessions I asked the minister to place in his estimates an amount sufficient to cover the installation of a water system in the reservation. A high percentage of the mortality in the reservation has been due to lack of hygienic conditions, the inhabitants having to get their water from the river. I have asked him further, to provide an amount for the rebuilding or the repairing of the hospital, which in fact is only an old stone building. At no place do I see any evidence of anything being done to implement the requests I have made.
Prior to last year the agent in the reservation was a gentleman named Lorenzo Letourneau. I do not know any man better qualified than he was to perform the duties he had to perform there. He is a highly educated gentleman with a large experience in municipal affairs, and moreover Mr. Letourneau not only fulfilled the functions of agent but the additional functions of distributing the relief in the whole reserve. For some unknown reason he was put out and there was appointed in his stead, without any public advertising of the position in my riding of Laprairie-Napierville, which should have been done in the normal course, a gentleman from the county of Two Mountains, the constituency of my hon. friend the Postmaster General. I have nothing to say

Supply-Indian Affairs
against the gentleman who was appointed, but I can certainly say this, that Mr. Letourneau had nobody superior to him to fill that position. It is true that when Mr. Letourneau was retired and this gentleman from Two Mountains was appointed, the Department of Indian Affairs also gave him a deputy or assistant agent, if I may call him such, who performed the functions of distributing relief in the Indian reserve of Caughnawaga. So to replace Mr. Letourneau they were obliged to appoint two men. Moreover, if I am well informed, they increased the salary of the Indian agent and gave a very high salary to the assistant agent. In view of the need for economy I am sure the hon. minister will agree with me when I say, without any undue reflection on the present administration, that certainly the government have no money to throw in the river, even in the St. Lawrence; but instead of keeping Mr Letourneau, who carried out the functions of Indian agent and relief agent, the government appointed in his place two men, one head agent at a higher salary and an assistant agent at a very big salary.
I would like to know from the minister what the reason was for retiring Mr. Letourneau on pension and replacing him with these other two gentlemen. What is incomprehensible is this, that whereas it was the usual thing whenever there was a change of administration in Ottawa and a vacancy occurred in this position, for the government to appoint as agent a citizen of the riding in which the reserve was situated in this case they appointed a gentleman from the riding of Two Mountains, in the county of my hon. friend the Postmaster General. I assume that the minister will reply that this position was filled by promotion. He may say that the agent being unable to perform his duty was retired on pension and replaced by a superior officer from another part of the country. But in answer to that let me say that to justify themselves the administration will have to prove that Mr. Letourneau was unable to carry out his duties. Although he had asked for help from the Department of Indian Affairs they gave him only a subagent or assistant agent, and then when the department finally retired Mr. Letourneau they concluded that the work he was doing required the services of two officers, so they appointed another gentleman with an assistant from another part of the country. The Department of Indian Affairs never offered any additional help to Mr. Letourneau, although he was strenuously overworked, and finally he was compelled by the department to retire on pension.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that in the circumstances an injustice has been done to that agent, unless the minister can explain satisfactorily why he was let out and another gentleman from Two Mountains appointed in his stead, with an assistant agent.
Before. I resume my seat I would remind the minister of a petition that he must have received from his own supporters in the riding of Laprairie-Napierville, or if he did not receive it, at all events the petition was sent to the Prime Minister from the Conservatives in the riding of Laprairie-Napierville protesting. very strongly against the appointment of a gentleman from outside the riding to the position of Indian agent. They claim that it was contrary to the custom, and insist that if the department was justified in relieving Mr. Letourneau he should have been replaced by a citizen of the county of Laprairie-Napierville.
To summarize I would like to know from the minister if anything has been done tc improve the relief system in the Caughnawaga reserve; has anything been done to improve the hospital situation; is there any amount in the estimates for repairing the hospital, and finally what was the reason for retiring Mr. Letourneau and taking on in his place a gentleman from the county of Two Mountains?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I find that there is an item of $200 in the estimates for the reconstruction of a bridge over the river Suzanne at St. Isidore which is in the Caughnawaga Indian agency. In regard to the hospital about which the hon. gentleman has asked a question, it is not a departmental but a private institution Over the years the department has assisted those in charge of the hospital in many ways, by cash grants and also by providing repairs and assisting in different directions in order that the hospital might fulfil its function. In fact, a very large sum has been spent by the department on this hospital.
What is the amount this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is nothing in the estimates for it this year. As regards the administration of the reserve, I stated a short while ago the amount of money we have placed in the estimates fort it: $3 465 for administration; $11,650 for medical services; $40,000 for relief; $1,800 for drainage, bridges and so on. I visisted the Caughnawaga reserve and met the former agent Mr. Letourneau, who lived at Ste. Constant, a village some twelve miles distant, where he carried on his private business as well as acting as Indian
Supply-Indian Affairs

agent for the reserve. I agree with the hon. member's remarks regarding Mr. Letourneau; I found him a very estimable gentleman. But that is not the point. The point is the proper administration of the reserve-and I did not say that it was improperly administered under Mr. Letourneau. But when the department is spending the amounts of money which are spent annually on that reserve, I think the hon. member will agree that it is a full time job; and Mr. Letourneau, having his private business to attend to, did not give his full time to the reserve, spending only two days a week there.
Was he ever required to give his full time to that work? If so, did he refuse?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not to my knowledge. But I consider that the administration of this reserve requires the services of a full time agent, and I may say that this is not the only reserve in Canada which demands the services of a full time man and which is not receiving it at the present time. Mr. Letourneau was retired, not because of any fault found with his services but in order that a better administration might be brought about. He had reached the retiring age, being sixty-seven or sixty-eight, and he was not in good health,
Did he ever complain?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not to my knowledge. The civil service commission were requested by the department to reclassify the agency, and on recommendation this was done and a promotional competition was held, which under the circumstances was, I think, the correct procedure. As a matter of fact that is what the civil servants of Canada state as one of the cardinal points of their policy, namely, that promotions should be held within the service wherever possible in order that those in the service may be encouraged in their work. The promotional competition was held by the commission and the present agent was appointed by the commission, not by the department, as stated by the hon. member. He has been provided with the services of a clerk, not an assistant agent, who is receiving SI,080 per annum; and under the present arrangement, with which I entirely agree, we expect to have a better administration of that reserve.

What was the salary of Mr. Letourneau when he was pensioned, and what is the salary of the gentleman who is now *gent in his stead?
fMr. Murphy.]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The former agent received $1,380 plus $300 allowance, making a total of $1,680. The present agent receives $2,100 per annum.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: To provide subsidies for wrecking plants, Quebec and British Columbia, $40,000.
How much of this is for Quebec and how much for British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine
speechtext: This appropriation is for subsidizing wrecking plants, one at Quebec and one at Victoria. The division between the two companies has not yet been made. I might say ito my hon. friend that the department has had a ten year contract with the Pacific Salvage Company, Limited, for a subsidy of $10,000 a year. This contract will expire in July next. We have had a yearly contract with the Quebec Salvage Company Limited for a subsidy of $30,000. This contract will expire next April. These subsidies are given in order to assure a perfect salvage service on the St. Lawmence and below the gulf by the Quebec Salvage Company and a similar service on the Pacific coast by the Pacific Salvage Company.
Would the min* ister tell the committee whether the Pacific Salvage Company at Victoria have made application for a renewal of the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine
speechtext:
They have made
application not only to renew the contract but to get a larger grant for years to come. We are now asking the committee to vote only $40,000, 'because we do not think we should increase these subsidies for this year. I cannot at present tell wha/t will be the division between the two companies. The Quebec Salvage Company Limited is insisting on getting at least the $30,000 voted and paid to it every year so far and is asking for more. On the other hand the Pacific Salvage Company Limited is also asking for more. I might tell my bon. friend that the Foundation Salvage Company, which has a plant at Halifax during the winter and also a small plant at Father Point during the summer, is asking for a subsidy. No decision has yet been reached as to what will be granted to the different companies out of the $40,000.

The reason I asked the question was that the Pacific Salvage Company prior to two years ago had a sub-station at Prince Rupert which is six hundred miles further north, and with the

Supply-Marine
increase in, shipping this is more needed now than it ever was ibefore. At that time the subsidy was not big enough so' that they had to take away the substation they had at Prince Rupert. As a consequence when anything happened to any boat on the northern coast around Prince Rupert they had to wait for the salvage boat to go the six hundred miles to tlhe wreck. Therefore I would sincerely urge upon the minister that when the renewal is made, consideration be given to the distances on the Pacific coast, the increase in shipping and the necessity of having more than one boat. At the present time the boat is stationed at Victoria, and if anything happens up north they have to send for the boat and depend on Providence to remain afloat until the boat arrives. The subsidy should be increased for that service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine
speechtext: The Department of Marine realizes the importance of having on all our shores sufficient salvage plants to satisfy the needs of navigation, but on the other hand those private companies are doing a fairly good business, especially on the Pacific coast where the salvage company operates the whole year round. I must say that the Pacific Salvage Company claim a deficit in its operations last year. The Quebec Salvage Company claims a larger deficit. As the latter company is operating only seven or eight months of the year, it does less business than the other firm and thereby suffers greater loss. That is the reason why the Quebec Salvage Company was getting a larger subsidy for some years past. I think my hon. friend is mistaken when he says that the Pacific Salvage Company does not maintain a plant at Prince Rupert. I understand from the company that they are maintaining a plant there.
It is a private concern that has a boat there, but there is no subsidy for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I understand that
at Vancouver they have two tugs, the Helac 1 and the Helac 2. They have in addition three powerful floating derricks. I understand that they have at Prince Rupert a salvage station, with derricks, diving gear and general salvage equipment.

It is a private
company that has done salvage Work and it used to do it under the direction of the Pacific Salvage Company, but I understand now that that company is not giving it any of the subsidy, so it is having quite a struggle to keep going.

Item agreed to.

The session before last I put a question to the minister as to what was being done about deepening the harbour of Montreal. At that time the minister gave me a very satisfactory answer when he said that a board of engineers and experts from the department had been formed to study the deepening of the harbour of Montreal between that city and lake St. Peter. Since then I understand work has been carried on by this board of experts, but the situation in the port of Montreal towards the end of the summer season when the water level is very low is important. Can the minister give any information to the committee, the citizens of Montreal and the shipping interests as to what progress is being made in this work of deepening the channel in the harbour of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine
speechtext:
As I told my hon.
friend at that time, a board of engineers composed of experts of the marine, public works, railways and canals and interior departments was formed with the object of ascertaining the cause of the lowering of the level of the St. Lawrence and the means of remedying that situation. This board has held many sittings since last year. Field operations have been carried on during the whole season of navigation, and now for nearly a month they have been working on an interim report. suffered at all from the fact that there has been no deputy minister in the past three years. In that case you might as well increase the salary of the acting deputy minister and of his first assistant, and why not do the same thing in the other departments? Here is one of the largest departments in the government, spending hundreds of thousands of dollars daily, and for three years it has got along without a deputy minister and things have been running smoothly, the minister says. We ought to know whether the time has not arrived when we should dismiss the idea of appointing a new deputy minister at all and get along with the services of the gentlemen who are now acting as deputy and assistant deputy. If they are giving good service their salaries might be increased and the position of deputy minister of the department abolished. If that is not the idea of the government, they should not delay any longer in deciding when the appointment is to be made. The Prime Minister has a program of reform, and he said that these reforms must start immediately. Well, this question has been hanging fire for the last three years, and each time I have asked the minister about it he has kindly and honestly said that it was the privilege of the Prime Minister to fill that office. But no doubt the advice of the minister also helps. The minister must give his opinion. The country is interested in knowing when this appointment is to be made. I am told that there are a good many candidates for the office and good officials, and the question is whether things are going to stay as they are, or if not, when is the vacancy to be filled?

It is very seldom, Mr. Chairman, that I take part in the discussions concerning the Department of Marine, but as the harbour at Montreal is in the riding which I have the honour to represent very humbly in this house, may I suggest to this country, because when a member speaks in this house he is speaking to the country at large, that it return at the next election the same Prime Minister, who will choose the same Minister of Marine who is now acting both as minister and deputy minister of his department with such great efficiency and such a saving to the country. He knows his department and is evidently a great administrator.

It is all very well to joke about this matter, but either the department needs a deputy minister or it does not. The present situation is almost a

public scandal, not only with respect to this position but the other vacancies which are awaiting appointments. No one regrets the Prime Minister's illness more than I do and that he is not able to be present in the house, but if he were in his place I would say the same as I am saying now, and that is that the government are taking very grave chances, because, if one is any judge of what is about to happen, they will not be in power very long, and it means that they are going to place a group of eighteen or twenty individuals in jeopardy, and that is most unfair to the men they appoint. It is unfair also to the officials of the Department of Marine who have been waiting for three years for a deputy minister. It is in fact a flaunting of authority, as this government has been doing in every direction since it has taken control of public affairs in this country. It is a public disgrace the way these matters are being treated, and the Minister of Marine cannot explain it away by saying it is the business of the Prime Minister to make the appointment. True it is the business of the Prime Minister. As I say, no one regrets his illness more than I do, but now that the matter is up we might as well say what we think about it. If it is the intention to retain this position of deputy minister of the Department of Marine for some member whose riding the government does not want to take the chance of opening- we might as well talk plainly-then I say all the more disgrace. But that is the situation as it appears not only to this side of the house but to this country generally. Moreover, there are officials surely in the department who are quite efficient to take charge of the department, and if the present assistant deputy minister has been able to carry on as stated by the minister, then surely he has some claim on the position. It is all very well to joke about it, but it is really no joke. Either you need a deputy minister or you do not. If it is a case of keeping the position open for some member on the other side and the government is afraid to let him resign and open his constituency and have a by-election, then all the more reason I say why this government should appeal to this country at once

The trouble extends beyond
an individual deputy minister; the whole civil service is honeycombed with the same thing. Positions have been abolished, possibly with the idea of economy; but somebody has to take the place left vacant and we find that men are put on temporarily. But you cannot get good work out of a temporary man who is likely to be fired on a change of government or for some other reason. And another

point to consider is that he is not contributing to the superannuation fund, so that by and by there will be a third of the service not contributing to it. It is not only one deputy minister here and there; it is the same thing right through the service down to some of the smaller officials. Every now and then the government says that all positions vacant at the moment will be abolished; but you are not abolishing a position if you have to fill it the next day. Some man is put on temporarily, receiving the regular salary, but he is not allowed to contribute to the superannuation fund. We find this everywhere-a man doing one man's job, a telegrapher, a doctor, and people of that kind. You must fill the job, and yet under the system that has been inaugurated these positions are left vacant. There must be scores of positions like that, and the morale and efficiency of the service are being destroyed. I am not talking about one man; I am speaking of the whole principle of leaving positions vacant, and I venture to say that if the various ministers asked their deputies frankly they would agree with me that it is demoralizing.

Mr. Chairman, I consider that this raise of salary to $8,000 is unjustified. In 1911, a senior clerk was in charge of the yard and his salary amounted to $2,800, I think. Mr. Lacouture succeeded him and received the same remuneration. Mr. Jackson succeeded Mr. Lacouture with a salary of $3,000. I want to call your attention to the fact that at that time 800 men were employed. From 1921 to 1930, the average number of men at work in the shipyard of Sorel was 800. There, in the centre of the province of Quebec, they are putting in charge a certain Mr. Carswell who does not understand a word of French. I say it is ridiculous, it is an insult to the province of Quebec. In Quebec, a man is not allowed to go on the bench if he does not understand French and English, and a man should not hold any position of government responsibility in Quebec if he does not speak and understand both languages. That is a principle I believe in. But to come back to my letter, what I said in it I believe in. It was not confidential, but was not intended to be made public; it was sent to my good friend the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge and I stand by what I said in it. I see across the aisle my good friend and ex-partner, the hon. member for Laurier-Outremont, one of the finest of men. He represents a great name and I know at the next election he is likely to be returned; with his name he cannot avoid it. But he is bilingual. When he came to this country he could speak only English. He has the advantage of having a great name; he belongs to a great family and now he can talk both languages. I hope this official in the Department of Marine, if he is going to get $8,000 a year, will learn French. That is my principle and will explain my letter.

When the question arose of this new appointment, because I believe it is actually a new one, at a salary of $8,000 a year, the minister was asked why this man was appointed. He stated that this man was appointed because they were making him permanent now on account of the saving he had made in the maintenance of the Sorel shipyard and matters connected with it. The minister ought to give us a further explanation. The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge, speaking in French, has stated that

not so much work is being done there; that fewer men are being employed than there were in past years, and that therefore there is not the same necessity for having such an expensive person in charge. Would the minister tell us what the expenditure has been since this man has been in charge? When did he take charge? Was it last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine
speechtext: This man was appointed acting superintendent in October, 1933.

So that he has been in
charge for over a year now?

speechtext: Yes.
Would the minister inform the committee what number of vessels, dredges and other boats have been repaired in 1932, 1933, and 1934, and the cost of each?
